9.1  Adequacy Made Measurable


Chapter 7 asked what a picture of a structure can carry, and Chapter 8 asked what a camera
does to it. This chapter fixes a single geometry and changes only how it is presented. The
development plan of this book states the governing idea as an inequality.  Given a full
state x, a reduced representation r(x), and a question Q, a procedure bQ that answers the
question from the reduced representation is adequate to the extent that

                             d Q(x), bQ(r(x)) ≤ε

over a stated domain of states. Here the state x is the geometry of the habitat of Chapter
3, the representation r is a presentation (a plan, an eye-level view, a cutaway, a wireframe),
the question Q is a property of the geometry that someone might want to know, and
bQ is whatever a reader, or a script standing in for a reader, does with the image. The
same presentation can be adequate for one question and badly wrong for another, so no
presentation is good in itself, and a statement about a presentation has the form: for this
question, on this geometry, with this reading procedure, the error is this large.

  The plan is to make the left side of the inequality computable in a few cases, so that
the habit of asking the question has numbers to attach to it. Two cautions apply. A
reading procedure must be specified before the error can be measured, and a human reader’s
procedure is not fully specified, so the procedures used here are simple automatic ones whose
failures are informative but not exhaustive. And ε comes from the purpose of the work, not
from the measurement: whether an error of 8 percentage points in a visible-floor fraction
matters depends on what the fraction will be used for.

def box(name, centre, dims, coll):
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=1.0, location=centre)
    o = bpy.context.active_object
    o.name = name
    o.scale = dims
    bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(location=False, rotation=False, scale=True)
    for c in o.users_collection:
        c.objects.unlink(o)
    coll.objects.link(o)

def build(entrance='centre', scene=None):
    scene = scene or bpy.context.scene
    coll = bpy.data.collections.new('Habitat')
    scene.collection.children.link(coll)
    g0, g1 = ENTRANCES[entrance]
    box('Platform', (0, 0, -0.2), (6.0, 6.0, 0.4), coll)
    box('Wall_North', (0, 2.9, H / 2), (6.0, T, H), coll)
    box('Wall_East', (2.9, 0, H / 2), (T, 5.6, H), coll)
    box('Wall_West', (-2.9, 0, H / 2), (T, 5.6, H), coll)
    box('Wall_South_West', ((-3.0 + g0) / 2, -2.9, H / 2), (g0 + 3.0, T, H), coll)
    box('Wall_South_East', ((g1 + 3.0) / 2, -2.9, H / 2), (3.0 - g1, T, H), coll)
    px, py = PLINTH['xy']
    sx, sy, sz = PLINTH['size']
    box('Plinth', (px, py, sz / 2), (sx, sy, sz), coll)
    bpy.context.view_layer.update()
    return coll, (g0, g1)

9.5 What the Experiment Does Not Show


The experiment used one geometry in two variants and one observer height, and the ques-

is a poor presentation in general or that a wireframe is poor; they answer different ques-

at a picture, and a person might use cues the procedure ignores, such as the convergence
of lines to read depth in the eye-level view. The measurement of false wireframe crossings
assumes that every crossing is a risk of misreading, which a practised reader may resolve
at a glance. The distance used, an absolute difference in a fraction or a position, is one
of many that could stand for d in the adequacy inequality. And the tolerance ε was never
specified, because it is a matter of purpose. The purpose of the habitat in this book is
to be revisited from several positions, which makes Question A the more relevant of the
two, and makes the plan, despite its excellent recovery of the entrance, the least adequate
presentation for it.

Chapter 10

Surface Treatment, Ornament, and
Essential Visibility



10.1  Ornament Is Relative to a Question


A surface treatment is anything done to the appearance of geometry without changing
the geometry: a colour, a texture, a bump pattern, a gloss, a shading model. Chapter 9
showed that a presentation is adequate or not relative to a question. The same holds for
the treatments applied within a presentation. A feature of a surface is ornament relative to
a question when removing it changes the answer a reading procedure gives by no more than
the tolerance ε of Chapter 9, and it is essential to that question when removing it changes
the answer by more. The definition is operational. It can be tested by rendering the scene
with and without the feature, applying the same reading procedure to both images, and
comparing the answers. And it is relative: a wood grain on a floor is ornament for the
question of where the entrance is and may be essential for the question of whether the floor
is timber.

  Ornament is not worthless, and the point of the definition is not to remove it. The point
is to know what each treatment costs and what it buys, so that a figure carries the ornament
its purpose can afford. A treatment can also cost something that is not decoration at all.
A noise pattern has no information about the plinth, and it can still damage a reader’s
ability to find the plinth. This chapter measures that damage in a simple case, shows that
its onset can be predicted from the colours alone, reports the cost in render time, which
proved undetectable, and shows what a shading model contributes beyond colour.


10.2 A Reading Task and a Noise Pattern


The task is to find the plinth in an oblique view of the habitat of Chapter 9, with the east
entrance. The reading procedure assigns each pixel to the nearest of four reference colours
(plinth, floor, wall, background), measuring distance in the CIE Lab colour space, in which
Euclidean distance approximates perceived colour difference. The distance between two
colours in Lab is written ∆E. The plinth is scored against a mask produced by rendering
the same view with flat identity colours, and the score is the intersection over union of the
pixels the procedure calls plinth with the pixels that are plinth. Precision is the share of
called pixels that are right, and recall the share of true pixels that are called.

  The ornament is a procedural noise pattern on the floor. A Noise Texture node, fed
with object coordinates, is rescaled by a Map Range node and drives a Mix node between
two tones of the floor colour, one darker and one lighter than the floor’s base colour by


                                       67

Chapter 10.  Surface Treatment, Ornament, and Essential Visibility


a relative amplitude a. At a = 0 the floor is flat, and at larger a it is a speckle whose
average tone stays at the base colour. The materials are emissive, so the pixel colours are
the assigned colours, and the experiment isolates the effect of the pattern from the effect
of lighting. The script is ornament.py.

  Three plinth colours were used. The distinct plinth is the blue of Chapter 7’s palette,
at ∆E = 58.1 from the floor’s base colour. The other two are the floor colour scaled up in
tone, by 1.15 and by 1.45, so that they have the same hue as the floor and differ in lightness
only; their distances from the floor colour are ∆E = 8.0 and 23.8. The tonal plinths are
the hard case, because the noise pattern moves floor pixels along exactly the line that joins
the floor colour to the plinth colour.

where errors begin and not how many there are. It is nevertheless the form of the useful
statement, which is a relation between the spread of the ornament and the separation of
the colours that carry the information.

10.4 What the Pattern Costs in Time

The flat emissive materials used above erase one thing the plinth has, which is its form. In

that are indistinguishable show a further point: a shading model gives information only
where the light makes surfaces differ, and a light placed so that two faces receive the same
illumination is a light that discards the distinction between them.



10.6 A Rule for Choosing


The measurements suggest a procedure for deciding how much surface treatment a figure
should carry. List the questions the figure is meant to answer, and for each, write the colour
or tone difference that carries its answer. Keep the separation between those colours larger
than the spread of any ornament that will share their region of the image, using a relation
such as a < (s −1)/2 as a first estimate and a rendered test as a confirmation. Then test
whether each treatment is ornament or essential by removing it and applying the reading
procedure, and keep the essential ones. What remains is a figure whose ornament was

def summarize(normals):
    n = len(normals)
    pts = vertices(normals)
    on = [[i for i, nv in enumerate(normals) if abs(nv @ p) < 1e-7] for p in pts]
    mult = [len(s) for s in on]

    return dict(V=V, E=E, F=F, chi=V - E + F, hist=dict(sorted(hist.items())),

12.1 A Curve Is a Recipe for Points


The construction of Chapter 11 drew nine circles as curve objects whose points were com-
puted by a script and stored as a polyline. Blender offers two further ways to store a curve,
and the choice among the three is a choice about what is exact and what is approximate.
A poly spline stores points and joins them by straight segments, so what is stored is already
the final shape, and its fidelity to a circle is set by the number of points. A Bezier spline
stores nodes, each with two handles, and defines a cubic polynomial between consecutive
nodes. A NURBS spline stores weighted control points and defines a rational curve. The
renderer does not draw either of the last two as such. It evaluates them to a polyline whose
density is set by the curve’s resolution, and the evaluated polyline is what a mesh conver-
sion, a bevel, or a ray test sees. A curve is therefore a recipe for points, and two questions
follow: how well do the points lie on the intended shape, and how many are needed?

   This chapter measures both for the circle, because the circle is the shape on which every
earlier chapter of this part depends, and because a circle has an exact definition against
which error can be computed. The measurements were made in Blender 5.2.2 with the
script curves_probe.py. The error reported throughout is the largest deviation from the
circle, or from the plane of the circle, over points sampled along every segment of the
evaluated polyline, nine per segment, so that the sag of a chord between vertices is counted
and not only the position of the vertices.




12.2 How Much Circle Is a Bezier Circle?


A circle cannot be a cubic polynomial, so a Bezier circle is an approximation by construction.
The standard construction uses four nodes at the quarter points, with tangent handles of
length κR, and the value of κ that makes each quarter arc pass through the circle at its
midpoint is 4 tan(π/8) = 0.552285. Blender’s own Bezier circle primitive uses handles of              3
length 0.552125, close to this and slightly shorter. A NURBS circle can be exact. Blender’s
NURBS circle has eight control points of order three with weights alternating between 1

and  2/2 = 0.7071, which is the rational form of the conic that is a circle, so its evaluated

12.5  Choosing a Representation


The measurements suggest rules of the following kind, each with its stated cost. When a
circle is generated by a script, a poly spline with N computed points places every vertex
on the sphere exactly and has a sag of R(1 −cos(π/N)), so the question is the tolerance of
the work. When a circle is drawn by hand, a NURBS circle is exact in its weights and costs
only the evaluation resolution. When a Bezier circle is required, because the curve must be
edited with handles, four nodes with the default handles give an error floor of 2.4 × 10−4,
and a larger number of nodes must be given tangent handles of the stated length or the
error will be several hundred times worse than the node count suggests. And when the
curve is to be a tube, the ring size is a second approximation that multiplies the first, with
the area ratio above.

13.1  Coordinates Are a Chart, and Vectors Are the Thing


Chapter 11 described a point of the sphere by a latitude β and a longitude λ, and a plane
through the origin by its unit normal. Those are two descriptions of the same objects, and
they have different properties. A pair (β, λ) is a chart: it covers the sphere except at the
poles, where λ is undefined and nearby points have very different longitudes. A unit vector
x = (cos β cos λ, cos β sin λ, sin β) has no singular point, and the distance, the great circle,
and the intersection of two circles are each one line of vector algebra. The practice adopted
in this chapter is to use coordinates to enter and report positions and vectors to compute
with them. The practice also has a numerical reason, because Blender’s mathutils vectors,
matrices, and quaternions store single-precision numbers, with a relative spacing of about
6 × 10−8, and a computation on them is only as good as its formula is conditioned.

  The mesh that Blender calls a UV sphere is the chart made into geometry. Its vertices lie
on parallels and meridians, with triangles at the poles, and its faces are therefore far from
equal in area. The table gives, for UV spheres of increasing resolution and for icospheres,
the vertex and face counts, the surface area and volume as fractions of the sphere’s values

13.4  Moving Along a Great Circle


Interpolating between two points on the sphere by the straight line between them and then
normalising the result keeps the point on the sphere and does not keep its speed. A uniform
step in the interpolation parameter moves the point fast near the middle of the chord and
slowly near the ends, and the effect grows with the angle between the endpoints. With 200
steps the ratio of the largest to the smallest angular step was 1.07 for endpoints 30◦apart,
1.99 for 90◦, 14.8 for 150◦, 130 for 170◦, and 9680 for 179◦. Spherical linear interpolation,
which weights the endpoints by sin((1 −t)θ)/ sin θ and sin(tθ)/ sin θ, gives equal angular
steps. The Vector.slerp method of mathutils had a step ratio of 1.0000 from 30◦to
170◦and 1.0015 at 179◦, with the largest departure of a point’s length from one at 10−7 to
10−6 up to 170◦and 5 × 10−5 at 179◦. An animated marker that follows a great circle by
normalised linear interpolation therefore appears to dwell at both ends, with a speed that
varies by a factor of two at 90◦, and the remedy is slerp or the formula above.


13.5  Stable Helpers


The three results of this chapter can be collected in a few lines. The function angle uses
the atan2 form, circle_normal refuses to return a normal when the points are nearly equal
or antipodal, and arc_point interpolates by the sine weights and falls back to normalised
linear interpolation for tiny angles, where the sine weights would divide by a vanishing
number.

13.6.  Counting From Floats




def angle(a, b):
    """Angle between two vectors from atan2(|a x b|, a . b); accurate for small and near-pi
     angles."""
    return math.atan2(a.cross(b).length, a.dot(b))



def circle_normal(a, b):
    """Unit normal of the great circle through a and b. Raises when a and b are (nearly)
    parallel."""
    n = a.cross(b)
    if n.length < 1e-4 * a.length * b.length:
        raise ValueError('points are nearly equal or antipodal; the circle through them is
    not determined')
    return n.normalized()



def arc_point(a, b, t):
    """Point at fraction t along the shorter great-circle arc from unit vector a to unit
    vector b."""
    th = angle(a, b)
    if th < 1e-6:
        return a.lerp(b, t).normalized()
    return (a * math.sin((1 - t) * th) + b * math.sin(t * th)) / math.sin(th)

Chapter 14

Parameterised Arrangements and
Their Boundaries



14.1 A Family Is a Map From Parameters to Structure


Chapter 11 introduced a family of nine-circle arrangements with two free parameters, the
azimuth offset α and the elevation β of the four flexible circles. A script that builds one
member computes a single instance. A family is the map from the parameters to what is
built, and the map has two kinds of output. The geometry, the positions of the circles and
vertices, varies continuously with (α, β). The combinatorial type, the numbers of vertices,
edges, and faces and the multiplicity of each vertex, takes finitely many values and changes
only at certain parameter values. The parameter plane is therefore divided into regions
on which the type is constant, which are the strata of the family, separated by boundaries
on which the type changes. Everything a reader needs to know about the family in order
to choose a member is contained in the list of strata, where the boundaries lie, and what
happens on them.

   This chapter maps the family numerically, examines how a boundary behaves when it is
approached, shows that the boundary that a computation reports depends on a tolerance
and not only on the geometry, and builds a generator that produces named members from
stored specifications and can be run twice without duplicating anything. The scripts are
param_sweep.py and fig14_boundary.py, and the numbers come from runs in Blender
5.2.2’s Python environment.

15.1  From a Rule to a Cluster


Part V studies structures that form without a plan: no part of the structure is placed by
a global design, and its shape results from many local events governed by a rule. The first
such rule is the simplest one that already produces a surprising object. A single site is
occupied. Particles arrive one at a time, wander at random, and stop when they touch the
structure. After a few thousand arrivals the structure is a branching cluster with long arms
and deep fjords, nothing like the compact blob that a naive picture of random deposition
suggests. The process is called diffusion-limited aggregation, and it is used here because it
is small enough to state completely and rich enough to show what a simulation can and
cannot establish.

  A rule is complete only when everything that affects the outcome has been stated. For
the version used here the statement is as follows. The sites are the integer points of the
plane, and the seed occupies the origin. Each walker starts on a circle of radius r +5 about
the origin, where r is the distance of the farthest occupied site, at the lattice point nearest
a uniformly random angle.  It moves one step along a coordinate axis, in one of the four
directions with equal probability.  If it ever stands at a distance greater than three times
its launch radius from the origin it is discarded.  If it stands next to an occupied site it
joins the cluster with probability p, the stickiness, and otherwise continues. Seven things
in that paragraph are choices: the lattice, the neighbourhood, the launch radius, the kill
radius, the step distribution, the sticking probability, and the random number generator
with its seed. Some of them are expected to matter for the result and some are expected
not to, and the point of the chapter is to find out which, by measurement.


15.2  The Rule as Code


The rule is short enough to read in full.





                                      99

Chapter 15.  Local Attachment Rules and What a Cluster Establishes




def dla_py(n, seed, p_stick=1.0):
    """Grow a cluster of n particles from a seed at the origin. One walker at a time starts
      on a circle just outside
    the cluster, takes unit steps along the axes, is discarded if it strays beyond three
     launch radii, and joins the
    cluster, with probability p_stick, whenever it stands next to an occupied site."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    occupied = {(0, 0)}
    order = [(0, 0)]
    r_max = 0.0
    while len(order) < n:
        r_launch = r_max + 5.0
        a = rng.random() * 2 * math.pi
        x, y = round(r_launch * math.cos(a)), round(r_launch * math.sin(a))
        kill = 3.0 * r_launch
        while True:
            dx, dy = ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))[rng.randrange(4)]
            x, y = x + dx, y + dy
            if x * x + y * y > kill * kill:
                break
            if ((x + 1, y) in occupied or (x - 1, y) in occupied or (x, y + 1) in occupied
     or (x, y - 1) in occupied) \
                    and (p_stick >= 1.0 or rng.random() < p_stick):
                occupied.add((x, y)); order.append((x, y))
                r_max = max(r_max, math.hypot(x, y))
                break
    return np.array(order)


   This version uses Python’s own generator and a set of occupied sites, and it is slow,
because a walker from a distance R needs of the order of R2 steps to reach the cluster.
The file dla.py also contains a version compiled with the Numba package that follows the
identical rule on an array, and the ensembles below use it. The two versions use different
random number generators, so they do not produce the same clusters from the same seed,
and the check is statistical. With 10 seeds each at N = 700, the exponent defined below
was 1.737 ± 0.118 for the Python rule and 1.692 ± 0.101 for the compiled one, where the
figures after ± are standard deviations across seeds. The difference, 0.045, is within one
standard error of the difference, 0.049, so the two versions agree to the precision of the test.

   Reproducibility inside one version was checked directly: the same seed gave the same
cluster, site for site, and a different seed gave a different one, with only 233 of 1500 sites
shared between seeds 5 and 6, mostly in the early core. The first five sites of seed 5 were
(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (1, 3). A cluster is therefore a function of the rule, its parameters,
the seed, and the version of the generator, and a record that omits any of these does not
reproduce it.

radius of gyration Rg(n), the root-mean-square distance of the particles from their centroid,
a compact cluster of the plane would have n ∝R2g and a one-dimensional string would have

16.1  Occupancy as a Rule


Chapter 15 grew a structure by adding one particle at a time. A second way of forming
structure without a plan keeps the lattice fixed and decides, for every site, whether it is
occupied. The simplest such rule treats the sites independently: each site is occupied with
probability p, by a draw that does not depend on any other site. The result is a random
field with a single parameter, and it is the starting point for two questions that matter
when the field is meant to be a space that someone can move through. The first is whether
the occupied sites, or the empty ones, form a connected region that crosses the whole grid.
The second is what a local rule applied repeatedly to the field does to its connectivity. This
chapter measures both on a square grid and then places the result in Blender as a habitat
floor plan, with the same attention to provenance as before.

   Four things have to be stated for the rule to be complete: the grid size n, the occupation
probability p, the notion of adjacency, and the generator with its seed. Adjacency matters
because it changes the answer. Two sites are four-adjacent if they share an edge and eight-
adjacent if they share an edge or a corner. A region of occupied sites is a set connected
through the chosen adjacency, and a region that touches both the top row and the bottom
row is said to span. All counts below use four-adjacency for connection of a region, and
the smoothing rule of Section 16.4 uses the eight sites around a cell.

  The code is in occupancy.py. The generator is NumPy’s default_rng seeded by an
integer, regions are labelled with SciPy’s ndimage.label, and a grid built twice from seed
7 at n = 64, p = 0.45 was identical site for site, while seed 8 differed from it at 2042 of
4096 sites. The occupied fraction of the seed-7 grid was 0.455 against a nominal 0.45, a
difference that is ordinary sampling variation, since the standard deviation of the fraction
over 4096 independent sites is 0.008.

16.4 A Local Rule Repeated


The standard remedy is a smoothing rule applied to every cell at once. A cell becomes
wall at the next step if at least five of the nine cells in its neighbourhood, itself included,
are wall, and becomes open otherwise; cells outside the grid count as wall. The rule is
synchronous, so the new grid is computed entirely from the old one. It is the majority rule
on an odd number of cells, so it has no ties. Repeated, it either reaches a grid that no
longer changes or it does not, and both outcomes occurred.

16 filled a lattice site by site. A third way of forming structure lets every existing element
produce its own successors, independently of the others. The simplest rule of this kind is
the Galton–Watson process. A single individual forms generation zero. Each individual
in generation g has a random number of offspring, drawn from one fixed distribution and
independently of every other individual, and those offspring make up generation g +1. The
record of who descended from whom is a rooted tree, and the tree is the object of interest,
because a branching structure in a habitat such as a drainage pattern, a root system or a
corridor network can be described in the same terms: a rule for how many children each
node has, and nothing else.

   For the version used here the offspring number is Poisson distributed with mean m. Four
things must be stated for the process to be reproduced: the offspring distribution and its
mean, the rule for stopping a run, the generator, and the seed. The stopping rule matters
more than it first appears. A process with m > 1 may grow without bound, and a process
with m ≤1 dies out with certainty, but in a finite computation a run can only be stopped,
and a run that has been stopped is not a run that has died out. The runs below stop at
extinction, at 60 generations, or when the tree reaches 20,000 individuals, and each run is
classified by which of the three happened. A run that reaches the size cap is counted as
a survivor in the estimates below, which is an approximation: a tree of 20,000 individuals
could in principle still die out, and the probability of that is small and was not measured.

  The code is in branching.py. The generator is NumPy’s default_rng seeded by an
integer. A run from seed 4 at m = 1.5 was identical on repetition, and seed 5 gave a
different tree.




17.2  The Extinction Law


The classical result is that the extinction probability q is the smallest non-negative solution
of q = f(q), where f is the generating function of the offspring distribution. For Poisson
offspring f(q) = em(q−1), and the solution is q = 1 for m ≤1 and a value below one for
m > 1. The solution was computed by iterating q ←em(q−1) from q = 0, which converges
to the smallest root, and then compared it with the fraction of runs that went extinct in
an ensemble of 2000 seeds at each m.

of a run into extinct, capped and alive must be reported, because the three outcomes are
different statements. And a result at the critical value of a parameter depends on the
stopping rule, so a figure such as 0.9605 is a property of the run length as much as of the
process.

Chapter 18

Foam-Like Cells and Relaxation



18.1  Space Divided Among Seeds



A third kind of cellular structure divides space instead of filling it. Given a set of points,
assign every location to the nearest point. The set of locations assigned to one point is
its cell, the cells are convex polygons in the plane, and together they tile it. The tiling is
the Voronoi diagram of the points. It describes, to a first approximation, the cells of a dry
foam, the territories of animals that defend the ground nearest their nests, the catchments
of wells, and the plan of a market in which each customer visits the nearest stall. In each
case the points are the primary data and the cells are a derived structure, so the useful
questions concern what the cells inherit from the points. This chapter asks what a random
arrangement of points produces, how an iterative rule that moves each point towards the
centre of its own cell changes the arrangement, and what can be measured to say so.

  To avoid edge effects, all arrangements are placed on a torus, the unit square with
opposite sides identified, and computed by tiling nine copies of the points and keeping the
cells of the central copy. The cells of the central copy are polygons that may extend past
the square, and together they cover it exactly once. The code is in foam.py. It uses SciPy’s
Voronoi, orders each cell’s vertices by angle about its point, and counts a side wherever
consecutive vertices are distinct. The generator is NumPy’s default_rng, and the same
seed gave the same points and the same side counts on repetition.





18.2 Two Identities That Hold for Every Arrangement



Two properties were checked on five random arrangements of 400 points before any statistics
were taken. The cell areas summed to 1, to the twelve decimals printed, so that the cells
tile the torus with neither gap nor overlap. The mean number of sides was 6 exactly, in
every arrangement. The second property is an instance of Euler’s formula. On a torus a
polygonal tiling has V −E + F = 0, and when three cells meet at every vertex, as happens
with probability one for random points, each vertex has three edges, so 2E = 3V and the
average cell has 2E/F = 6 sides. The identity says nothing about the points, and it holds
for the regular hexagonal tiling and for the most irregular one alike.  It follows that the
mean number of sides cannot distinguish arrangements, and the quantities that can are the
spread of the side counts and the spread of the cell areas.

All results are for points on a torus, with 400 points in the tables and 150 in the Blender
scene, and with 20 seeds for the statistics, so edge effects, which dominate small real foams,
were excluded by construction. The relaxation rule was stopped at 50 steps, and nothing
was measured about its limit. The side-count and area spreads for random points are
compared with literature values that are recalled from reading. The linear relation of area
to number of sides was observed over a pooled sample and not tested for other densities
or for relaxed arrangements. Nothing here shows that a real foam, a territory pattern or a
market follows the Voronoi rule, which assigns each location to the nearest point and ignores
the surface tension, the competition and the travel costs that govern the real systems. The
experiments show what a nearest-point rule does with random and relaxed points, with the
precision stated.

19.1 A Network That Responds to Its Own Load


The preceding chapters of Part V formed structures from rules of attachment, occupancy,
branching and division. A structure that carries something, such as water through channels,
nutrients through a fungal mat, or traﬀic through streets, raises a further question: what
happens when the carrying capacity of each link responds to how much it carries? Slime
moulds, vein networks and river basins are often described in these terms, and a short rule
of this kind is simple enough to state completely, run, and check in Blender. This chapter
uses the rule to close Part V and to introduce the coupling between a numerical solver and
a scene that Part VII develops.

  The network is a square grid of 16×16 nodes with 480 unit-length edges. Each edge e has
a conductance De. One corner node injects a unit of flow and the opposite corner removes
it. Given the conductances, the flow is fixed by conservation at every node together with
Ohm’s rule that the flow in an edge equals its conductance times the pressure difference
between its ends. That is a linear system, solved here by direct elimination with the sink
grounded at zero pressure. The conductances then adapt: each is moved towards a function
of the flow it carries,

integrated by explicit steps of 0.3. The exponent µ is the one free parameter and controls
how strongly a loaded edge is reinforced. For µ = 1 the reinforcement is linear in the flow
for small flows, for µ > 1 it is disproportionately strong for busy edges, and for µ < 1
weak edges are reinforced relatively more. A rule of this form is used in models of the
slime mould Physarum, as recalled from reading and not rechecked, and the precise form
above is an assumption of this chapter and not a reproduction of a particular paper. Initial
conductances are 1 plus noise of standard deviation 0.05, clipped below at 0.5, drawn from
a seeded generator. The code is in transport.py.

Chapter 20

Inspecting a Scene and the Two
Ways to Act on It



20.1 Why Python Changes the Kind of Work


Part V ran every experiment from a script, and the scripts shared habits that were never
stated: they built objects from data, they put generated objects in collections of their
own, they checked what the scene held, and they could rebuild it from a seed. Part VI
states those habits as a method. Blender’s Python interface offers two ways to act on a
scene that look alike in a short example and behave very differently in a long program. One
imitates the interface: an operator such as bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add does what
the menu item does, using the current selection, the active object and the active collection.
The other edits the data directly: bpy.data.objects.new creates an object and nothing
else. This chapter measures the difference, shows what each leaves behind in the scene,
and builds two small tools, an inventory of what a scene contains and a way of clearing
generated content without touching anything else.  All measurements were made in the
headless Blender 5.2.2 used throughout, with a factory-reset empty scene at the start of
each probe. The scripts are scene_tools.py and ch20_probe.py.


20.2  Three Parts of the Interface


The module bpy has three parts that matter here. The first, bpy.data, holds every data-
block in the file as named collections: objects, meshes, materials, collections, cameras and
so on.  It is a database, and it is available whatever the interface is doing. The second,
bpy.context, describes the present state of the interface: the active object, the selected
objects, the current scene and mode.  Its contents change as operators run. The third,
bpy.ops, is the set of operators, each a command that reads the context, makes changes
and may fail if the context does not suit it. A script that mixes these without noticing
which it is using will behave differently when run from a different starting state.


20.3 What Each Leaves Behind


A cube was created by operator in an empty scene and a triangle was created by the data
interface, and the scene was examined before, between and after. Before anything, there
was no active object, no selection, and no objects or meshes. After primitive_cube_add,
the new object was active and selected, its mesh was named Cube, and it belonged to
the scene’s master collection and not to the collection named Generated that the script


                                      123

Chapter 20.  Inspecting a Scene and the Two Ways to Act on It


had made. After the triangle was created with bpy.data.meshes.new, from_pydata and
bpy.data.objects.new, the active object was still the cube, the selection still held one
object, and the triangle was in Generated because the script linked it there. The opera-
tor therefore changes the interface state and places the result by context, while the data
interface changes what it is told to change.

   Operators  also depend on a context that may be absent.   In an empty  scene,
bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='EDIT')  raised a RuntimeError with  the message
“Operator bpy.ops.object.mode_set.poll() Context missing active object”, and after a
cube had been added it ran and put the object in edit mode. The failure is a poll failure:
each operator first asks whether the context permits  it. A script that depends on an
active object must establish one, and a script that never uses an operator never meets the
question.


20.4 What Names Are and Are Not


A name is a label for a data-block within its collection and it is not a stable identity. Three
objects created with the name Wall were named Wall, Wall.001 and Wall.002. When the
first was removed and a new object was requested with the name Wall, the new object
received the name Wall, the freed name, and the existing objects were Wall, Wall.001 and
Wall.002 as before. A record that says “the object called Wall” therefore refers to a different
object after the sequence than before. A script that must find its own objects later should
record something that survives, such as the generated collection they were placed in, a
custom property holding an identifier of its own, or the parameters from which they can
be rebuilt, which is the approach of Chapters 15 to 19.


20.5  Orphans


Removing an object does not remove its mesh. After a mesh with one user was linked into an
object and the object was removed through bpy.data.objects.remove, the mesh was still
in bpy.data with zero users. The call bpy.data.orphans_purge(do_recursive=True)
then removed it, and returned 1. Whether a zero-user block survives a save is a separate
question, and it was tested: a mesh with no users was written to a file and was absent
when the file was read back, while a mesh with the fake-user flag survived. An orphan is
therefore harmless to a saved file and a nuisance to a running session, where it remains
listed in the data and keeps its name in use.


20.6 Two Small Tools


The two tools are short enough to read in full.





                                          124

20.6. Two Small Tools




"""Chapter 20: inspect a scene and keep generated content in one removable collection."""
import bpy


GEN = 'Generated'



def inventory():
    """Counts of data-blocks by type, with how many have no users (orphans)."""
    out = {}
    for attr in ('objects', 'meshes', 'materials', 'collections', 'cameras', 'lights', '
    images', 'node_groups'):
        blocks = getattr(bpy.data, attr)
        out[attr] = (len(blocks), sum(1 for b in blocks if b.users == 0))
    return out



def generated_collection(scene):
    """The one collection that scripts may fill and clear; created on first use and linked
    to the scene."""
    coll = bpy.data.collections.get(GEN)
    if coll is None:
        coll = bpy.data.collections.new(GEN)
        scene.collection.children.link(coll)
    return coll



def clear_generated(scene):
    """Remove only the objects in the generated collection, and the meshes that only they
    used."""
    coll = generated_collection(scene)
    meshes = {o.data for o in coll.objects if o.type == 'MESH'}
    for o in list(coll.objects):
        bpy.data.objects.remove(o)
    for me in meshes:
        if me.users == 0:
            bpy.data.meshes.remove(me)


  The inventory returns, for eight kinds of data-block, how many exist and how many have
no users.  It is the first thing to print in a script that misbehaves, and the second is the
same inventory after the script has run, because a difference between them is a complete
account of what the script changed at the level of data-blocks. The second tool concerns
cleanup. The generated collection is the only place the script puts its objects, and the
clearing function removes only the objects in that collection and the meshes that no one
else uses once they are gone.

  The clearing function was tested on a scene with a hand-made object called Mine on
a mesh called Keep, outside the generated collection, and fifty generated objects sharing
one mesh. Before clearing, the scene held 51 objects and 2 meshes. After clearing it held 1
object and 1 mesh, Mine and its mesh were intact, and a second call changed nothing. A
third case put one generated object and one hand-made object on a common mesh. After
clearing, the common mesh was still present, with one user, because the function removes
a mesh only when its user count has fallen to zero. This is the property that matters: a
cleanup that removes by name or by type would have deleted the hand-made work, and


                                          125

Chapter 20.  Inspecting a Scene and the Two Ways to Act on It


one that removes by collection and by user count cannot.



20.7  The Cost of Imitating the Interface


The two approaches differ in speed as well, and the difference grows. Creating 300 unit
cubes by operator took a median of 2081 ms over five repetitions, with the repetitions
ranging from 2041 to 2677 ms, or about 6.9 ms per cube. Creating 300 objects that share
one mesh through the data interface took a median of 3.9 ms, with a range from 3.7 to 4.7
ms, about 13 µs per object. The ratio of the medians was about 540. These timings are
from one machine with software rendering and should be read for their order of magnitude,
as stated in the scope of the book.

  The operator’s cost per cube is not constant. For 50, 100, 200 and 400 cubes the medians
of three repetitions were 47, 190, 810 and 4464 ms, which is 0.94, 1.9, 4.1 and 11.2 ms per
cube. Doubling the number of cubes multiplied the total time by 4.0 at first and by 5.5
at the largest step, so the cost of the loop grows faster than the count. The reason was
not investigated; a likely cause is that each operator updates the whole scene and so costs
more as the scene grows, but that is a guess. The data interface grew far less: for 300, 1200
and 4800 objects the medians were 3.7, 24 and 117 ms, or 12, 20 and 24 µs per object, so
the per-object cost rose by a factor of two over a sixteen-fold increase in count. A loop of
the size used for the clusters of Chapter 15, which had 3000 objects, would take at least
half a minute by operator even at the per-cube rate measured for 400 cubes, and the true
figure would be larger since the rate rises with count, and about 0.07 seconds by the data
interface at the rate measured for 4800 objects. The operator figure is an extrapolation
and was not run.



20.8 What These Experiments Do Not Show


The measurements are from one build and one machine, in headless mode with no interface
drawing. The behaviour of operators in a running interface, where a redraw follows each call,
was not measured. The context failure was shown for one operator, and the clear-up tool
was tested on three constructed cases and not on a file produced by a long working session.
The cause of the growth in operator cost is a guess. Names were shown to be reused in one
sequence, and the full rules for name allocation were not studied. Nothing here argues that
operators should never be used. Some operations, such as applying a modifier or a boolean
operation on selected objects, are most conveniently done by operators, as far as is known
here, and the sensible practice is to use the data interface for construction and operators
for the few operations that need them, with the context established deliberately.

21.1  Building from Arrays


Chapter 20 established that construction by the data interface is cheap and leaves the scene
alone. This chapter turns to what is built. A mesh is stored as arrays: vertex positions, a
list of loops that each name a vertex, and polygons that each name a run of loops. Blender
offers a convenient entry point, Mesh.from_pydata, that takes ordinary Python lists, and
a lower-level one, foreach_set, that  fills each array from a flat buffer. The second is
what a program that has already computed its geometry in NumPy should use, because
the geometry arrives as arrays and need not be turned into lists of tuples and back. The
function in mesh_tools.py builds a mesh of equal-sided faces in that way, and a second
function reports the facts a script should check before trusting any mesh it has made.





                                      128

21.2.  Is the Lower-Level Route Worth It?




"""Chapter 21: build meshes from arrays, and check what was built."""
import numpy as np
import bpy, bmesh



def mesh_from_arrays(name, verts, faces):
    """verts: (n,3) floats; faces: list of equal-length index tuples (all triangles or all
    quads), built with foreach_set."""
    verts = np.asarray(verts, dtype=np.float32); faces = np.asarray(faces, dtype=np.int32)
    k = faces.shape[1]
    me = bpy.data.meshes.new(name)
    me.vertices.add(len(verts)); me.vertices.foreach_set('co', verts.ravel())
    me.loops.add(faces.size); me.loops.foreach_set('vertex_index', faces.ravel())
    me.polygons.add(len(faces))
    me.polygons.foreach_set('loop_start', np.arange(0, faces.size, k, dtype=np.int32))
    me.update(calc_edges=True)
    return me



def report(me):
    """Facts about a mesh that a script should check before trusting it."""
    bm = bmesh.new(); bm.from_mesh(me)
    nonmanifold = sum(1 for e in bm.edges if len(e.link_faces) > 2)
    boundary = sum(1 for e in bm.edges if e.is_boundary)
    out = dict(V=len(me.vertices), E=len(me.edges), F=len(me.polygons), L=len(me.loops),
               euler=len(me.vertices) - len(me.edges) + len(me.polygons), boundary_edges=
    boundary, nonmanifold_edges=nonmanifold,
               area=round(sum(p.area for p in me.polygons), 6))
    bm.free(); return out


  The report gives the counts of vertices, edges, faces and loops, the Euler characteristic
V −E + F, the number of boundary edges, the number of edges shared by more than two
faces, and the total face area. Each of these is a statement that can be compared with what
the construction was meant to produce, and the chapters of Part V used them in this way.

21.3 What validate Finds and What It Does Not


A mesh can be built from indices that make no geometric sense, and the interface will
often accept it. The method Mesh.validate checks for structural errors and repairs them,
returning a true value if it changed anything. It was applied to six constructed cases.


         Case                   Before (V,E,F)  Returned  After (V,E,F)

           clean quad                          4, 4, 1        false           4, 4, 1
           face repeating a vertex             4, 4, 1        true           4, 3, 0
           duplicate face                       4, 4, 2        true           4, 4, 1
           loose vertex                         5, 4, 1        false           5, 4, 1

named the same vertex twice together with one of its edges, and removing the duplicate
face. It left alone the three cases that are structurally valid and geometrically doubtful: a
vertex with no face, a triangle whose three points lie on a line, and two faces that meet
along a pair of coincident but unmerged vertices, so that what looks like a shared edge is
really two. These are the faults that matter in a generated structure, since each makes

the coincident pair shows as boundary edges where a shared edge was intended, and the
degenerate triangle as a total area of zero. The loose vertex is not exposed by the report as
written, which has no count of unused vertices, and Exercise 21.2 asks for one. A validator
of the interface cannot know what the construction intended, and the script’s own checks,
which compare the build with its specification, are the ones that can.

The order in which a face lists its vertices decides which side is its front. A cube was built
with every face written outward and again with every face reversed. The signed volume
computed from the faces was +1.000 for the first and −1.000 for the second, and the nor-
mals of the second pointed towards the centre. Applying recalc_face_normals to the
second mesh restored a signed volume of +1.000. A volume taken from a mesh is therefore
meaningful only after the orientation has been checked, and a script that sums mesh vol-

21.5  Attributes


Data attached to a mesh, such as the number of sides of each cell in Chapter 18, are stored
as attributes on a named domain. For a four-vertex square, a floating-point attribute on
the point domain had four values, one for each vertex, and an integer attribute on the
face domain had one. A colour attribute had four components per element.  Setting an
attribute from a buffer of the wrong length failed with an error that named the expected
and received lengths and an internal error in the call, so the length of the buffer is checked
by Blender. Asking for a second attribute with a name already in use did not replace the
first. It created an attribute named with a numeric suﬀix, so two attributes were present
and the original name still referred to the first. A script that creates attributes in a loop
without checking for existing ones will accumulate them, as the generated names showed.



21.6  Where Precision Goes


Positions are stored in single precision. A vertex requested at a distance X from the origin
plus a small offset d was read back, and the offset recovered was as follows, in the same
units.

                          105       0.000    0.0078   0.1016

and a hundredth became a little under a hundredth. At a million units a hundredth was
lost and a tenth became an eighth. The spacing of representable numbers at 105, 106 and

The consequence for construction is that positions should be built near the origin and in
units that keep the structures of interest within a few thousand units, and that a quantity
needing finer resolution than the spacing at its distance must be stored in the data, as an
attribute or a property, and not in the position. A structure placed far from the origin
does not lose its shape gradually; its smallest features simply cease to exist.

22.1 A Constructor Is a Function From a Specification


Chapters 20 and 21 made single objects. A habitat needs many objects of one kind, with
members that differ in a few parameters, and a way to say afterwards what each member
is. This chapter builds the smallest useful machinery for that: a constructor that takes a
specification, refuses a specification that makes no sense, builds the object, and records on
the object what it was built from. The example is a staircase of n solid steps, each with
a rise, a run and a width. It is chosen because its volume, height and depth are known in
closed form, so that the construction can be checked against formulas and not only against
itself. Step k occupies the run from (k −1) run to k run and has height k rise, so the volume
is width · rise · run · n(n + 1)/2, the height is n rise and the depth is n run.

  The code is split in two files. stairs.py contains no Blender code: it validates a specifi-
cation, computes vertices and faces, and hashes geometry. stairs_blender.py builds the
mesh in Blender, places the object in the generated collection of Chapter 20, and records
provenance. The division means that the part of the constructor that decides the geometry
can be tested without Blender, and that the Blender part is only a translation.

22.2  Refusing Bad Specifications


A specification is a dictionary with exactly four entries. The validator rejects a missing
entry, an unknown entry, a count that is not a whole number or lies outside 1 to 200, and
a dimension outside 0.01 to 100. It was tried on seven faulty specifications and rejected all
seven, each with a message naming the entry at fault: n = 0, n = 2.5, a negative rise, a
missing width, an unknown key colour, n given as the Boolean true, and a rise that is not
a number. The last two deserve a remark. In Python a Boolean is an integer, and a value
that is not a number fails every comparison, so a test written as “reject if the value is out
of range” would let both through. The validator is written as “accept only if the value is
within range”, which is the safe form because it rejects what it does not understand. The
bounds themselves are choices. They stop a typing mistake from creating a million faces
and they are not claims about what a staircase may be.

Each object made by the constructor carries four custom properties:  the name of the
constructor, a version number, the specification as a text string with keys in sorted order,

and a short hash of the geometry actually stored in the mesh. The hash is a SHA-1 digest
of the vertex coordinates rounded to five decimals and the face lists, shortened to twelve

to the mesh, accidental or intended, changes the hash.

was not tested, and that matters because single-precision conversions and the face order
produced by the interface could differ; the version number on the object is the place to
record that a rule has changed.


22.5  Making a Constructor Safe to Call Twice


A script that creates objects is often run again, after an edit or after a failure. A constructor
that makes a new object each time produces duplicates. The function ensure looks in the
generated collection for an object made by this constructor with the same specification
text and returns it if found, and makes a new one otherwise. The comparison is by the
specification string and not by the name, because Chapter 20 showed that names are reused.
Called twice with one specification it returned the same object both times and the object
count did not change. A new specification created one object, and the same specification
written with its keys in a different order returned that object and made none, because the
stored text sorts the keys.

  Changing a specification is a separate operation. The function update builds a new mesh
from the new specification, assigns it to the existing object, rewrites the stored specification
and hash, and removes the old mesh if nothing else uses it. After an update from n = 7
to n = 9, the object was the same object, the number of meshes in the file was unchanged,
the stored specification showed n = 9, and the rebuild check passed. Identity is thereby
kept across a change of parameters, which is what a habitat needs when a stair is made
longer and everything that refers to it should still find it. Whether anything else refers to
the object, and how, is a design question for Part VII.

one machine and its stability across builds is unknown. The ensure function compares
specifications by their text, so two specifications that differ by a float that prints the same
would be treated as the same, and the validator does not round. Nothing was tested about
concurrent edits, about objects modified by hand after generation, or about files saved and
reopened with the constructor’s objects in them. A hand-modified object keeps its recorded

Batch Generation and the Manifest



23.1  From One Object to a Family


A constructor that makes one staircase becomes a way of exploring a design when it is
called many times with different specifications. The questions that arise are those of any
batch process. How are the specifications chosen, and can the choice be reproduced? What
happens when one of a hundred specifications is wrong? How much of the work can members
share? And what record must exist so that the family, and not only each member, can be
rebuilt? This chapter answers them for the staircase constructor of Chapter 22 using the
file batch.py, which builds a family from a seeded sampler, writes a manifest, and verifies
the manifest in a fresh process.

  The sampler draws each of the four parameters independently from a short list: n from
3 to 14, three values of rise, three of run, and three of width, so there are 12 · 3 · 3 · 3 = 324
distinct specifications. The draws come from Python’s random.Random seeded by an integer.
The list is deliberately small. Members with equal specifications then share one mesh, as
the cluster sites of Chapter 15 shared one cube, and the effect of sharing can be counted.
Member i is placed on a grid, 25 to a row, at a pitch of four units, so that its position is a
function of its index alone.

23.1. From One Object to a Family




def sample_specs(count, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [{k: rng.choice(v) for k, v in CHOICES.items()} for _ in range(count)]



def place(i, per_row=25, pitch=4.0):
    return ((i % per_row) * pitch, (i // per_row) * pitch, 0.0)



def build_family(specs, scene=None, on_error='stop'):
    """Validate every specification first. on_error='stop': build nothing if any is invalid
    . 'skip': build the valid ones."""
    scene = scene or bpy.context.scene
    cleaned, errors = [], []
    for i, sp in enumerate(specs):
        try:
            cleaned.append((i, validate(sp)))
        except ValueError as e:
            errors.append((i, str(e)))
    if errors and on_error == 'stop':
        return [], errors
    coll = generated(scene); cache = {}; members = []
    for i, sp in cleaned:
        key = spec_json(sp)
        if key not in cache:
            cache[key] = build_mesh(sp, 'Stair')
        me = cache[key]
        o = bpy.data.objects.new(f'Stair {i:04d}', me); o.location = place(i); coll.objects
    .link(o)
        o['constructor'] = 'make_stair'; o['version'] = VERSION; o['spec'] = key; o['index'
    ] = i; o['geom_hash'] = mesh_hash(me)
        members.append(dict(index=i, spec=json.loads(key), geom_hash=o['geom_hash'],
    location=list(place(i))))
    return members, errors



def manifest(members, seed, count):
    body = dict(constructor='make_stair', version=VERSION, seed=seed, count=count, members=
    members)
    text = json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True)
    body['manifest_hash'] = hashlib.sha1(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    return body



def verify(man):
    """Rebuild every member from the manifest alone and compare geometry hashes; returns (
    agree, total)."""
    bpy.ops.wm.read_factory_settings(use_empty=True)
    members, errs = build_family([m['spec'] for m in man['members']])
    ok = sum(1 for a, b in zip(members, man['members']) if a['geom_hash'] == b['geom_hash']
     and a['spec'] == b['spec'])
    body = {k: v for k, v in man.items() if k != 'manifest_hash'}
    h = hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    return ok, len(man['members']), h == man['manifest_hash'], errs

Chapter 23.  Batch Generation and the Manifest


23.2 When One Specification Is Wrong


The function validates every specification before it builds anything. Two policies for a bad
specification are offered. Under the first, stop, a batch containing any invalid specification
builds nothing and returns the errors. Under the second, skip, the valid members are
built and the errors are returned beside them. The two were compared on a batch of 50
specifications in which three were corrupted: member 7 had n = 0, member 20 a negative
rise, and member 41 no width. Under stop no object was built, the generated collection
held none, and the three errors were reported with their indices and messages. Under skip
forty-seven objects were built, the same three errors were reported, and the members kept
the indices they had in the batch, so the built indices ran 0 to 6, then 8 and 9.

  The choice between them is a decision about what a batch means. If the family is only
valid as a whole, as when a street of stairs is meant to be continuous, a partial family is
worse than none, and stop is right. If members are independent samples, the valid ones are
worth keeping, and skip is right provided that the errors are not lost. Validation before
building is common to both, since it prevents the third possibility, a family half built before
the first failure and left in the scene.


23.3  Counting What Is Shared


With 324 possible specifications, a batch of N draws contains fewer distinct members than
N. For N = 200 and seed 5 there were 145 distinct meshes in the scene for 200 objects, and
for seed 6 there were 148.  If every specification were equally likely and independent, the
expected number of distinct specifications among 200 draws is 324 [1 −(1 −1/324)200] =
149.4. The two observations lie within a few of that figure. The number of meshes in
Blender equalled the number of distinct specifications in every case, so the cache works as
intended, and a family of many objects costs as many meshes as it has distinct shapes.

   Larger batches approach the limit. For N = 100, 1000 and 5000 the number of distinct
specifications was 91, 318 and 324, so 5000 objects shared 324 meshes, and the whole
possible family was present. Timing came from three repetitions in a fresh factory-reset
scene each time. The median time to build was 25 ms, 248 ms and 1001 ms, with the range
over repetitions 24 to 25, 213 to 288 and 931 to 1009 ms, which is about 250, 250 and 200
microseconds per member. The cost per member is roughly constant over a fifty-fold range,
in contrast to the growth of the operator loop in Chapter 20, and a batch of five thousand
members takes about a second on this machine. As elsewhere, the timings are for orders
of magnitude on one machine.


23.4  The Manifest


The record of a family is a text file containing the constructor, its version, the seed, the
count, and one entry per member with its specification, geometry hash and location, to-
gether with a hash of the whole body. For N = 200 and seed 5 the manifest was 26,940
bytes. Generating the family twice, in two separate runs of Blender, gave byte-identical
files, and a different seed, 6, gave a different manifest, whose hash was 5dce27454cf7 against

e6e0d5b70f8e for seed 5.

construction is deterministic on one machine and that the manifest holds what is needed. It
does not show that the seed alone would regenerate the same specifications on every version

not use the seed. That is a reason to store the specifications and not only the seed. The
manifest’s hash detects any change to the file, which includes accidental editing but does
not detect a change made together with a recomputed hash.


23.5 What These Experiments Do Not Show


The family has four parameters with a short list of values each, and the batches had at
most 5000 members. The failure test used three corrupted specifications in one batch.

during building and not during validation, or about members changed after generation.
The agreement of the distinct-mesh counts with the probabilistic estimate rests on two
seeds at N = 200 and on three batch sizes, and is a consistency check and not a test of the
sampler’s quality. The manifest was verified on the machine that made it. Verification on
another machine or another build of Blender is the real test of whether it is a record, and
was not done.

Chapter 24

Separating Geometry,  State, Pre-
sentation, and Input



24.1  Four Layers


A fly-through animation shows a place and an interactive world is one that can be changed
and revisited, and the difference is not a matter of rendering. A world that persists has
something in it that changes and remembers, and when the same program must also be
drawn and driven by someone, four responsibilities have to be kept apart. The authored
geometry is what was built by hand or by a constructor: the layout, the edges of a network,
the walls of a room. The state is everything that changes as the world runs: the quantities
attached to each element, together with whatever is needed to continue the process. The
presentation is the picture, a function that takes the geometry and the state and produces
an image. The input is what someone or something outside the process does to it, here a
list of events. This chapter builds the smallest world in which the four are separate and
measures what the separation buys and what it does not.

  The process is the adaptive network of Chapter 19: a 16 × 16 grid with a source and a
sink, conductances that adapt to the flow, and µ = 1.5, at which the network settles on a
single path of 30 edges. Two kinds of event are added: a cut forces an edge’s conductance
to a floor of 10−6 from that step on, and a restore lets it adapt again. The state is a
conductance for each edge, a flag for each edge saying whether it is cut, and a step counter.
The code is in world.py, which contains no Blender code, and world_blender.py, which
builds the geometry once and provides a presentation function that sets the width and
colour of each edge from a state and renders. The state lives only in world.py. The scene
holds geometry and the properties that the presentation function writes, and nothing the
process would need to continue.


24.2  Replay and Restart


Because the state and the events are plain data and the update is deterministic, a run is a
function of the initial seed, the log of events, and the number of steps. A log of three events,
a cut of edge 220 at step 100, a cut of edge 321 at step 160, and a restore of edge 220 at step
220, was run to step 400 twice in separate processes, and both runs gave the same hash of
the final state, f95eb316fd70. The hash covers the conductances as eight-byte floats, the
cut flags and the step counter.

  A world that is stopped must be resumable. For a different log, a cut at step 100 and a
restore at step 220 on the same edge, the state was saved at step 150 as raw bytes, reloaded,

and run on to step 400 with the same log. The hash equalled that of the uninterrupted run,
08869aa15643. A checkpoint that left out the cut flags, keeping only the conductances,
resumed to a different state, 641593f391d8. The conductances alone do not determine the
future, and a record of the world that stores them without the flags is incomplete in a way
that does not announce itself.


24.3  History Is Part of the State


Two worlds with the same rules and the same current inputs need not be in the same state.
Edge 220 lies on the settled path. In one world it was cut at step 100 and restored at step
150, and in the other nothing was done. At step 300 both worlds had 30 kept edges and
no edge cut, but the set of kept edges differed, with a largest difference in conductance
of 0.50, and at step 1200 the difference was unchanged. The cut had made the network
choose another path, and it did not return. When two cuts were applied in the opposite
order, edge e2 at step 100 and edge e1 at step 160 instead of the reverse, the final hashes
differed, although the kept edge set was the same. What the world is now depends on what
has been done to it, and a record that holds only the present appearance cannot say what
the world would do next. The log of events is therefore part of the world’s record, as the
seed was part of the cluster’s in Chapter 15.


24.4  Where the State Is Held


If the scene were the only holder of the state, it would be stored in single precision, as
Chapter 21 showed, and the process would continue from rounded values. To measure
what that costs, the same process was run for 400 steps in double precision and in a version
that rounded every conductance to single precision after every step. The largest difference
in conductance at the end was 9.0 × 10−8 at µ = 0.8, 2.3 × 10−5 at µ = 1.2 and 3.0 × 10−8
at µ = 1.5, and the sets of kept edges were the same in all three cases, with 480, 76 and
30 edges. For this process, then, a state held in the scene would behave the same to the
precision of the readings. That result belongs to this process. It is a contraction towards a
fixed point, and a process that amplifies small differences could behave otherwise. A scene
that is the only holder of state also disappears when it is deleted, and a state held outside
is unaffected, as the next section shows.


24.5  The Presentation Is a Function of the State


The presentation function reads a state and writes a width and a flow value on each edge
object, then renders.  It was tested in four ways, with the state at step 300 of the plain
run. Rendering twice left the state’s hash unchanged, so presentation does not alter state.
All objects and collections in the scene were then deleted, the geometry was rebuilt from
build_geometry, and the same state was rendered again: the pixels were identical to those
of the first render. The scene, in this sense, is disposable: deleting it loses nothing that the
state and the authored layer cannot restore.

24.6 What the Picture Cannot Show



The presentation is not a faithful copy of the state, because widths of 0.06 + 0.9D cannot
resolve conductances far below the width of a pixel. At step 300 the conductances of the

  A cut earlier in the run behaves differently. Cutting the same path edge at step 10, 20,

one can recover from a cut while the other cannot. The threshold between a conductance
of 10−42, which cannot recover, and 10−12, which can, was not located. This is a property
of the model, whose reinforcement vanishes for unused edges. The lesson for building a
world is general: a state must be inspected through measurements of what it can do, and
a picture of it does not show every difference that matters.

Chapter 24.  Separating Geometry, State, Presentation, and Input


24.7  Input as Events


Input has been treated throughout as a list of events, each with the step at which it applies,
and the process never reads the scene to learn what was done. A person using a mouse
would produce the same events, appended to the log by a layer that translates clicks into
edge numbers, and the presentation would then redraw. The separation lets the same world
be driven by a script, a test, or an interface. It also makes the events inspectable: the log
that produced the hash f95eb316fd70 is three lines. What the separation does not provide
is any statement about responsiveness. Nothing here measures how fast a click could be
turned into an update and a redraw, and a world that is interactive in the sense of the
book’s plan needs that measurement in the runtime that will host it.



24.8 What These Experiments Do Not Show


The world is one process on one grid with one seed, and two kinds of event. The replay and
restart results are deterministic comparisons on one machine, and the hashes depend on
the byte layout of this build and have not been compared on another. The comparison of
single and double precision covered three exponents and one seed. The finding that renders
vary at several samples comes from a small number of renders of a few scenes, six or eight
each, and the cause was not identified, and it should not be read as a statement about the
engine in general. The conductance threshold below which an edge cannot recover was not
located, and the model’s behaviour under repeated cuts was not explored beyond the cases
shown. No interactive input was tried.

25.1 What an Export Promises


A world that is meant to be explored, managed or simulated at length may be run by a
program other than Blender, and what Blender then supplies is geometry, materials and
records. The hand-over is a file, and a file is a contract that neither side states fully. This
chapter asks what is in the file. No game engine or viewer was available in the working
environment, and none is used. The checks are made instead with a short reader of the
binary glTF format, glb_read.py, which parses the container, the JSON description and
the binary buffer without Blender and without any rendering. The reader is an independent
check in a limited sense. It can say what was written, and it cannot say what any particular
engine will do with it. The experiments were run with Blender 5.2.2 and its bundled glTF
exporter, and with its OBJ exporter for comparison.

"""Minimal independent reader for binary glTF (.glb): no Blender needed. Used to check what
      an exporter wrote."""
import json, struct
import numpy as np


CT = {5120: np.int8, 5121: np.uint8, 5122: np.int16, 5123: np.uint16, 5125: np.uint32,
     5126: np.float32}
NC = {'SCALAR': 1, 'VEC2': 2, 'VEC3': 3, 'VEC4': 4, 'MAT4': 16}



def read(path):
    data = open(path, 'rb').read()
    magic, version, length = struct.unpack('<4sII', data[:12])
    assert magic == b'glTF' and version == 2 and length == len(data)
    off = 12; js = None; bn = b''
    while off < length:
        clen, ctype = struct.unpack('<II', data[off:off + 8]); chunk = data[off + 8:off + 8
      + clen]; off += 8 + clen
        if ctype == 0x4E4F534A:
            js = json.loads(chunk.decode())
        elif ctype == 0x004E4942:
            bn = chunk
    return js, bn



def accessor(js, bn, i):
    a = js['accessors'][i]; bv = js['bufferViews'][a['bufferView']]
    n, k = a['count'], NC[a['type']]; dt = np.dtype(CT[a['componentType']])
    start = bv.get('byteOffset', 0) + a.get('byteOffset', 0)
    stride = bv.get('byteStride', k * dt.itemsize)
    if stride == k * dt.itemsize:
        arr = np.frombuffer(bn, dtype=dt, count=n * k, offset=start).reshape(n, k)
    else:
        arr = np.stack([np.frombuffer(bn, dtype=dt, count=k, offset=start + j * stride) for
      j in range(n)])
    return arr.copy()

(1, 3, −2), (4, 0, 0), (0, 0, −5) and (0, 6, 0), so a point (x, y, z) in Blender appears as (x, z, −y).

25.6  Reading It Back


The staircase of 12 steps was exported, imported into a fresh scene, and compared with the
original. The importer produced 156 vertices and 100 triangles where the original had 52
vertices and 28 faces, two of them non-convex 26-sided caps. The set of distinct positions
was the same as the original’s, 52 points equal to 10−5 after the axis change was undone.

imported triangles in their imported orientation gave 3.071250, the formula’s value. The
method of Chapter 21, which recalculates the orientation of every face and then computes

imported mesh has separate vertices for every face, so its faces are not connected to each
other, and the recalculation, which chooses the outward side by looking at neighbours,
flipped some faces arbitrarily. After the coincident vertices were merged, 156 to 52, the same
recalculation gave 3.071250. The result sharpens the caution of Chapter 21: orientation can
be recalculated only for a surface whose faces are connected, and a mesh from an importer
should be merged before it is trusted.

precision, the vertex splitting and the triangulation were observed and not studied across

Chapter 26

Identity and Returning to a Site



26.1 A Visit Is a Reference


A visitor who walks through a world and later wants to return to a place has made a
reference to it. Strategic play, navigation by landmark, and a record of what has been seen
all depend on the reference finding the same place again after the world has changed. This
is an identity problem and not a drawing problem. The previous chapter treated a world
as state, authored geometry and presentation. A place is an element of the geometry and
the state, and the question here is what a record must say about it so that, after the scene
is regenerated, edited, reordered or copied, the record still names that place and no other.

   Six ways of referring to one of the staircases of Chapter 23 are compared. A reference by
name records the object’s name in the scene. By order it records the object’s position in
the collection. By index it records the generation number stored on the object. By location
it records the position in space. By content it records the specification and the geometry
hash of Chapter 22. By identifier it records a twelve-character code assigned to the site
once, from the seed and the index, and stored in the family’s record as well as on the object.
The code is in identity.py. A bookmark holds all six, and each resolver uses only its own.
A hidden property named truth follows each site through every change and is used only to
score the result: a resolver is correct if it finds exactly one object and that object is the
site, wrong if it finds exactly one and it is another site, ambiguous if it finds more than one,
and missing if it finds none.

26.3  Reading the Table


No reference by an attribute of the scene survives every change. Name fails completely under
renaming, order under shuffling, index under insertion. Location fails under insertion too,
since in this family a member’s position is computed from its index, and it fails for exactly
the sites that were moved, 62 of 200. Each of these attributes is correct until the one thing
that it depends on changes, and the dependence is rarely written down. A name depends
on nobody renaming, an index on nobody inserting, a position on nobody moving. Each
dependence is an assumption about the world’s future, and a persistent world has to expect
that the assumption will be broken.

   Content is not identity.  In the control, where nothing had changed, only 48.5% of
bookmarks resolved by content, because 103 of them matched more than one object. The
family has 145 distinct specifications among 200 members, so many sites are exact copies
of others and nothing about their shape or parameters distinguishes them. A reference by
what a place looks like is a reference to a kind of place. Changing a parameter made it
worse, with 17 results wrong, 76 ambiguous and 38 missing, since a site whose specification
was edited into another site’s specification matched that site.

  An identifier survives when it is assigned once and kept outside the scene. It was correct
in every row in which the family’s record supplied it, which includes insertion and shuffling,
where all the other schemes fail.  It failed completely when the regeneration did not use
the record and assigned fresh identifiers: 200 of 200 bookmarks were missing. An identifier
stored only on the objects is lost when the objects are rebuilt, and it must be stored where
the objects are built from, which is the manifest of Chapter 23.

   Duplication defeats identifiers too. Copying an object copies its custom properties, so
the copy carries the original’s identifier and index.  In the run of the table the twelve
duplicated sites became ambiguous for the identifier and the index, 94.0% resolved, while
name and location remained correct because the copies had new names and new places. In
a separate run with a fresh generator that duplicated more, 23 identifiers were each held by
two objects, and 23 objects carried a numeric suﬀix on their names. A persistent identifier
needs a check for uniqueness that is run after any operation that can copy, and a rule for
what a copy is: a new site that needs a new identifier, or a second view of the same site
that shares one.
